body: Six houses stand in a terrace and four of them are still open to the sky. Twenty to seven on a Thursday, and a bricklayer is standing in the middle of the row. Somebody from the site office has been round with a roll of masking tape and a marker pen, and every door frame that exists now has a number on it — 14, 16, 18 and so on up the row, stuck to bare timber. The postman comes past on his way to the finished end of the street, looks at the tape, and says he will be delivering to number 18 in October. Nobody laughs, because he is not joking.

That is not a fiction and nobody there treats it as one. The address exists before the house does, because the address is what the house gets built into. Getting the number down first is how anything larger than a shed gets made.
Of the 121 frequencies on this band, 46 are live and playing at this moment. The rest are assigned, named, described and in build. That is deliberate rather than embarrassing.

It is also the oldest arrangement in broadcasting, and worth taking literally rather than treating as an excuse. Nobody has ever been granted a frequency for a station that already existed. It runs the other way about: a regulator issues a licence and a place on the band to somebody who has undertaken to build something and put it there, and that somebody then goes away and builds it, sometimes for years, while the number waits with their name against it. The licence is the commitment. The transmitter is only the consequence. Every station anybody has ever loved spent a stretch of its life as a number on a piece of paper and a promise about what would go out on it.

The band runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70. Every station holds one frequency, no two share a number, and nothing here is ever renumbered — which is why a link somebody shared a year ago still lands exactly where it was pointed.

That rule costs more than it looks. A number held for a station still in build cannot be handed to a live one that is doing well, and cannot be quietly recycled when the build takes longer than anybody hoped. There is no version of this dial on which the popular frequencies spread out into the space the unfinished ones occupy. The band is therefore full of held numbers a product manager would want back, and they are not given back, because what is being kept is not a slot in a list. It is a place for something promised. The dial you tune next month will not be the dial you tuned today, and that is the plan rather than an apology.

Saying in public what does not exist yet has gone out of fashion, for reasons anyone can understand. The habit now is to ship quietly and withdraw quietly: no roadmap, because a roadmap can be held against you; no announcement, because an announcement dates; and when something is discontinued it simply stops appearing. None of that is dishonesty. It is what an industry does once it has learned that the only unforgivable thing is to be visibly late. The cost is that nothing can be waited for any more, and a person with nothing to wait for has no particular reason to come back.

The band is partitioned the way a broadcast band is — a five-fold stretch for the ministry stations, a long multilanguage run for the nations, the mainstream formats grouped together. The frequencies in build are not parked at the far end where they would be tidily out of the way. They sit among the live ones, so the dial fills in rather than extends, and the gap between two stations somebody already uses is very often the next thing to arrive.
There is an obvious alternative to all of this, and it deserves a fair hearing before it is dismissed.

It is to say nothing until everything is finished. Launch complete, no silent numbers, nothing to explain and nobody disappointed on a Tuesday. That is a tidier product and it makes for a far better opening week. What it cannot survive is the arithmetic of its own catalogue: a band of this size is years of writing, checking and clearing, and a rule that nothing goes out until all of it is ready means the first listener waits on the last station. It also decides quietly which languages go first, since the way to shorten a launch is to cut the frequencies with the fewest people behind them — precisely the ones nobody else was ever going to build.
A number held in the open is a promise. A plan kept private is only an intention.

A man of sixty-one is closing a kitchen at half past ten at night, in a town he came to when he was thirty-one. The chairs are up, the fryer is off, his nephew is doing the floor with a phone propped against the till. It is worship music, which is not unusual in that kitchen. What is unusual is that it is in Vietnamese — not an English chorus with Vietnamese words fitted over the top, which he has heard plenty of and does not care for, but singing written that way to begin with. He asks the boy to put it back to the start. He does not say anything else about it. He finishes the sink, and the song goes round twice more before the lights go off.

Nothing in that kitchen required a translation department or a decade of fundraising. It required a number kept free for a language no commercial broadcaster was ever going to allocate one to, and somebody getting round to filling it.

Most of this band is not there yet, and that is the plain state of it. You can read a description, see a frequency, know the format and the hours it will keep, and find it is not playing, because it does not exist to play yet. Build queues slip. The station you would most want is as likely to sit in a later phase as an earlier one, and no amount of interest from you moves it up by itself. Anybody who promises a schedule this size will land exactly as drawn has never built one.

The silence is the honest version. A service that keeps its unfinished work out of sight looks complete and tells you nothing, and you cannot know whether the thing you wanted is coming next year or was abandoned in a meeting. Publishing the gap is the only arrangement anybody can be held to. A number you can see, with a name and a description against it, is something somebody can be asked about later, and being able to ask later is very nearly the whole of what a promise is.

So this is not a finished product with holes in it. It is a site with the addresses already up. The tooling underneath keeps improving, and that compounds in a way that is easy to underestimate: every advance in generation, in translation and in voice makes the next station cheaper to build than the one before it, so the list of languages and formats that are out of reach gets shorter every year rather than longer. A great deal of what was plainly impossible when this band was laid out is now merely queued.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial and it helps to know they are there. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. The live ones are playing now, the rest are numbered and coming, and both sit on the same dial.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 337.70 — Vietnam Inspire. It is an odd recommendation for an English-speaking reader and that is precisely why it is the right one here: you will not understand a word of it. What you will hear is worship written in Tiếng Việt rather than translated into it, on a frequency that would never have survived a commercial argument anywhere else, and that was a held number on this dial long before it was a station. Put it on for ten minutes while the kettle boils. It is this entire article in audible form — something that exists because a place was kept for it, playing for people who are not you.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation to come back rather than a launch to attend. Tune it this afternoon, and then tune it again at the end of the month and go looking for a number that was quiet the last time. Some of them will still be quiet. One or two will not, and there will have been no announcement, because a station signing on is not news here — it is simply the address finally having a house on it.
